test.purpose: A report regenerated from the saved record is byte-identical to the live one, with the reachability and global-state sections included.

test.name: HLR-032: a global-state finding survives the round trip
test.purpose: The verdict and its participants are carried in the record, and the citation is derived from the verdict on both paths rather than stored.

test.name: HLR-080: Ca and Ce match the hand-computed table
test.purpose: The three components' afferent and efferent couplings and their Instability values match the table worked out by hand in the fixture header.

test.name: HLR-080: a repeated call does not raise efferent coupling
test.purpose: One caller invokes the same component twice. Coupling counts components depended upon, not calls made, so the repeat must not move the figure — without it the fixture would pass against an implementation counting call sites.

test.name: HLR-082: instability is Ce over Ce plus Ca
test.purpose: The bottom layer is depended on by both others and depends on nothing: 0.00, and a real number rather than undefined.

test.name: HLR-082: a component with both couplings zero is undefined, not zero
test.purpose: The division the requirement forbids. Reporting 0.00 there would claim maximum stability for a file with no relationships at all.

test.name: HLR-080: every component appears, not only the interesting ones
test.purpose: The table lists every component rather than only those crossing a threshold, which would make it a finding list.

test.name: HLR-081: no component is a bottleneck at the default threshold
test.purpose: Asserted so the flag has to be earned: a suite that only ever saw a flagged component would pass against an implementation flagging everything.

test.name: HLR-081: a component is a bottleneck when both couplings meet the threshold
test.purpose: Lowering the threshold produces the flag, and the component with zero efferent coupling stays clear — the rule is both couplings, not either.

test.name: HLR-099: the bottleneck threshold is marked as elc's own heuristic
test.purpose: The finding names the threshold as elc's own rather than citing a standard it does not have.

test.name: HLR-081: the threshold is configurable and appears in the heading
test.purpose: The value in force is stated in the report, so a reader knows what the flags were judged against.

test.name: HLR-083: a cycle between two components is reported as an ordered loop
test.purpose: The loop is reported in order and closed, so the reader sees which edge to cut rather than only which files are entangled.

test.name: HLR-083: the same pair is a recursion finding as well
test.purpose: Mutual recursion across two files is legitimately both: one statement says the stack depth has no finite bound, the other that the files cannot be built or understood apart.

test.name: LLR-CYC-03: mutual recursion within one file is NOT a component cycle
test.purpose: The case HLR-083 calls out by name. A file does not depend on itself, so the component projection holds no loop.

test.name: LLR-CYC-03: that same file still reports the recursion
test.purpose: Paired with the test above so that an implementation detecting nothing anywhere cannot pass it.

test.name: HLR-083: an acyclic project reports no cycles
test.purpose: No cycle is invented where none exists.

test.name: HLR-079: a call bypassing an intervening layer is skip-level
test.purpose: A call descending two layers is reported with both endpoints and the layers crossed.

test.name: HLR-118: a call inverting the declared direction is reported separately
test.purpose: A call ascending one layer is reported as a direction inversion, with its own kind.

test.name: LLR-LAY-03: the two are distinct findings, each without the other
test.purpose: One call skips without inverting and the other inverts without skipping. An implementation folding them into a single layering violation fails here, and so does one reporting a skip only when the call also inverts.

test.name: HLR-079: a call descending exactly one layer is not reported
test.purpose: The arrangement the user declared produces nothing, so the findings above have to be earned.

test.name: HLR-079: the layers crossed are reported with the finding
test.purpose: The ordinal distance travels with each finding, since the requirement asks for the layers crossed and not merely that some were.

test.name: HLR-078: the declared order determines the direction
test.purpose: Declaring the same layers bottom-up inverts every judgement: the call that skipped downward now ascends two layers and is both findings, and the one that inverted now descends one and is nothing.

test.name: HLR-078: --stratum-order states the direction explicitly
test.purpose: The order option corrects layers declared in the wrong sequence, and may be given before them.

test.name: HLR-063: --stratum-order naming an undeclared layer is a usage error
test.purpose: A misspelt layer name ends the run rather than silently leaving the layering measured against something else.

test.name: HLR-063: a partial --stratum-order is a usage error
test.purpose: A partial order determines no direction, and silently completing it would invent one.

test.name: HLR-063: a malformed stratum declaration is a usage error
test.purpose: A declaration that cannot be parsed ends the run with the fatal status and a diagnostic.

test.name: HLR-115: with no strata declared the analysis is omitted with a reason
test.purpose: The heading states the omission rather than leaving an empty table to read as a clean architecture.

test.name: LLR-CTR-09: omitting layering does not omit the coupling table
test.purpose: A run with no strata still reports coupling and instability for every component.

test.name: LLR-ARC-04: a stratum matching no component is diagnosed and retained
test.purpose: Retained rather than dropped: dropping it would renumber the layers below and change what the remaining calls are compared against, turning a typo into a wrong answer.

test.name: HLR-094: a component in no declared stratum is outside the partition
test.purpose: With only one layer declared, the calls touching undeclared files produce nothing.

test.name: HLR-032: the architecture sections survive a record round trip
test.purpose: A report regenerated from the saved record is byte-identical to the live one, with the coupling, cycle and layering sections included.

test.name: HLR-032: a cycle and its loop survive the round trip
test.purpose: The ordered loop and the coupling figures come back from the record, neither being recomputable without a graph.

test.name: HLR-086: each boundary value classifies into exactly one band
test.purpose: The three boundaries that produce findings band as the published table says.

test.name: HLR-086: the bands below the warning threshold produce nothing
test.purpose: Five of the eight boundaries are silent. An implementation banding 8 and 10 as warnings would pass the test above and fail this one.

test.name: HLR-086: the acceptable band is silent, not a gap
test.purpose: The 8-10 range produces no finding, which is the band an earlier reading of the thresholds left out.

test.name: HLR-086: exactly three findings come out of the boundary file
test.purpose: The count catches a band claiming a value twice, which a per-value assertion would not.

test.name: HLR-031: a measurement inside its band is still reported
test.purpose: A fan-out of 10 produces no finding and is still in the fan-out table. The findings list is the subset that crossed a line, never a replacement for the measurements.

test.name: HLR-099: every finding names its source
test.purpose: No finding row is emitted without a source column, and the fan-out rows cite Henry-Kafura.

test.name: HLR-099: recursion is attributed to MISRA C Rule 17.2
test.purpose: The safety standard the recursion finding rests on is named in the report.

test.name: HLR-099: a single-function global is attributed to MISRA C Rule 8.9
test.purpose: The global-state verdict carries a severity and the published rule that draws the line.

test.name: HLR-099: the bottleneck threshold is marked as elc's own
test.purpose: The one threshold that is not a published standard says so where it is read, which is what keeps the no-built-in-opinion claim honest while shipping MISRA and Martin values beside it.

test.name: HLR-099: no published threshold is labelled as elc's own
test.purpose: Paired with the test above: the marker appears on the row that earns it and nowhere else.

test.name: HLR-084: every dependency cycle is reported at critical severity
test.purpose: The acceptable count of cycles is strictly zero, so each is critical.

test.name: HLR-123: every finding carries a severity from the closed set
test.purpose: No row carries a severity outside info, warning and critical.

test.name: HLR-123: findings are ranked most severe first
test.purpose: Critical rows precede warning rows, because the list exists to be worked from the top.

test.name: HLR-100: severity does not move the exit status
test.purpose: A project reporting critical findings still exits 0 when every file was read. The exit status is reserved for failures; deciding what a finding warrants is the caller's business.

test.name: HLR-100: the summary counts findings without gating on them
test.purpose: The counts are figures to read rather than gates to pass, and the run still succeeds.

test.name: HLR-098: a project inside every band reports no findings
test.purpose: A project whose every measurement sits inside its accepted range produces an empty findings list.

test.name: HLR-031: the empty Findings section is still emitted
test.purpose: The heading appears with nothing under it, because an absent section is indistinguishable from a renderer that forgot.

test.name: HLR-101: no finding proposes a fix
test.purpose: No finding contains imperative remediation text. elc reports where a measurement falls and which standard says so, and stops there.

test.name: HLR-032: findings survive a record round trip byte-identically
test.purpose: A regenerated report is byte-identical to the live one with the findings section included.

test.name: HLR-056: a regenerated report keeps each finding's attribution
test.purpose: The citation cannot be re-derived on regeneration, which has no measurements to band, so the record carries it.

test.name: HLR-085: fan-out is exact at every band boundary
test.purpose: Fan-out is correct for 2, 3, 7, 8, 10, 11, 15 and 16 distinct callees — the values Phase 12 will band, asserted individually so a failure names the boundary that moved.

test.name: HLR-085: a repeated call does not raise fan-out
test.purpose: Every caller in the fixture invokes one helper twice; the figures are unchanged, which is what the whole boundary table rests on.

test.name: HLR-085: a function that calls nothing has fan-out zero
test.purpose: A leaf reports zero rather than being omitted.

test.name: HLR-085: every function appears, not only the interesting ones
test.purpose: All twenty-four functions are listed: this is a measurement table, not a finding list.

test.name: HLR-087: the hand-counted depth matches
test.purpose: The four-layer chain measures four.

test.name: HLR-088: the deepest chain is reported in full, in order
test.purpose: The ordered sequence from entry point to deepest leaf is reported, not merely its length.

test.name: HLR-088: the deepest branch is taken, not the first
test.purpose: The entry point calls the shallow branch first; the reported chain is the deep one, so the traversal is a longest-path search and not a first-path one.

test.name: HLR-087: the depth is presented with the unresolved count
test.purpose: The depth heading states the unresolved count, so the figure is read as the lower bound it is.

test.name: HLR-089: direct and mutual recursion are both reported
test.purpose: One decomposition finds both kinds, and labels which is which.

test.name: HLR-089: the recursive functions are named
test.purpose: The members of each cycle are named, since MISRA C Rule 17.2 is about which functions are involved.

test.name: HLR-090: recursion yields no depth figure, and the run terminates
test.purpose: A recursive graph reports unbounded depth with no chain, and the run completes — a longest-path search over it would not.

test.name: HLR-090: no finite depth is invented for a recursive graph
test.purpose: No layer count appears anywhere in the report for a recursive graph.

test.name: HLR-115: with no entry points, depth is omitted with its reason
test.purpose: The run succeeds and the report states that no entry points were declared, rather than reporting an empty or zero result.

test.name: HLR-115: an omitted depth does not omit the other measurements
test.purpose: Fan-out is still reported when the depth analysis is omitted; omitting one analysis does not silence its neighbours.

test.name: HLR-095: main is not inferred, however obvious it looks
test.purpose: A file containing an obvious entry point still omits the analysis, because entry points are declared and never guessed at.

test.name: HLR-115: an entry point matching nothing is a distinct omission
test.purpose: A declared symbol matching no analysed function produces its own omission message, distinct from having declared none.

test.name: an unmatched entry point is diagnosed on stderr
test.purpose: The unmatched symbol is named on standard error, and the run still succeeds.

test.name: HLR-032: two runs over the same tree agree
test.purpose: Two runs produce identical reports.

test.name: HLR-033: the targets may be given in either order
test.purpose: The report does not depend on the order the targets were named in.

test.name: HLR-056: the measurements survive a record round trip
test.purpose: A report regenerated from a record is byte-identical and still carries the depth, since none of the call-tree measurements can be recomputed without the source.

test.name: HLR-102: the emitted call tree renders under Graphviz
test.purpose: Validity is settled by handing the file to Graphviz and requiring it to render, never by matching text that looks like DOT — the first artefact elc produces for another program to read deserves the reader's own verdict.

test.name: HLR-102: the recursive tree renders too
test.purpose: The second tree renders as well, so the annotations only it carries cannot have broken the syntax.

test.name: LLR-STY-02: stripping every annotation leaves the same valid tree
test.purpose: The degradation claim tested by performing the degradation: every attribute is deleted from the file, and what is left must still render and must still hold the same twenty-five nodes and nineteen edges.

test.name: HLR-103: the call tree is written without being asked for
test.purpose: The companion appears with no option naming it, which is the default the requirement states.

test.name: HLR-103: --no-dot suppresses it
test.purpose: The report is still written and the companion is not, so declining the artefact costs the run nothing else.

test.name: HLR-104: no call tree is written when the report goes to stdout
test.purpose: With no output path there is no name to derive, so nothing is written and no default name is invented.

test.name: HLR-104: still none on stdout with generation disabled
test.purpose: "Whether or not generation was disabled" is the requirement's wording, so both routes to the same absence are asserted: the destination decides it, not the switch.

test.name: HLR-119: the companion is named from the report by substitution
test.purpose: An output of analysis.md yields analysis.dot rather than analysis.md.dot, and the companion takes no path of its own.

test.name: HLR-119: the .dot and the GraphML are siblings of one report
test.purpose: Both companions derive from the same output path in one run, which is what makes the naming rule one rule rather than two that happen to agree.

test.name: the tree holds one cluster per source file and every function
test.purpose: Six clusters and twenty-five nodes, matching the hand-worked table: the drawing accounts for every function the report does.

test.name: LLR-DOT-04: nodes are emitted in ascending identifier order
test.purpose: This is the one renderer that walks the graph rather than the sorted report model, so it must impose its own order; without this the graph library's internal enumeration would reach the output.

test.name: LLR-DOT-04: each node's adjacency is in ascending target order
test.purpose: The second half of the same guarantee, on the edges rather than the nodes.

test.name: HLR-032: two runs over the same tree produce an identical call tree
test.purpose: Byte-identical across runs, which is what the imposed ordering exists to deliver.

test.name: only call edges are drawn; a shared global is not a call
test.purpose: The artefact is the call tree. Two functions joined by a shared global and by nothing else have no edge between them; their coupling reaches the drawing as a property of each node instead.

test.name: HLR-105: the deepest call chain is annotated, nodes and edges
test.purpose: Six functions and the five steps between them. The chain lies inside the accepted band, so it is annotated because it is the chain and not because it warned — which is the case a fixture built only from findings would miss.

test.name: HLR-105: every unreachable function is annotated
test.purpose: All seven, including the four that call one another in a region no path from the entry point enters — reachable and connected are different properties.

test.name: HLR-105: a fan-out over the band is annotated with its severity
test.purpose: Eleven distinct callees is the first value that warns, and the drawing carries the catalogue's severity rather than a view of its own.

test.name: HLR-105: both participants in a hidden channel are annotated
test.purpose: The writer and the reader, neither of which calls the other. HLR-105 asks for the participants, so the annotation is on the functions rather than on an edge.

test.name: HLR-105: two findings on one node ride two attributes
test.purpose: A function that both takes part in a hidden channel and is unreachable shows both, because each annotation takes a different Graphviz attribute. One overwriting the other would make a drawing silently incomplete.

test.name: HLR-105: every member of a dependency cycle is annotated
test.purpose: Both components, not only the one the catalogue files the finding against: a finding has one subject and a set has no single location, and the requirement asks for the members.

test.name: HLR-105: a bottleneck component is annotated and attributed
test.purpose: The coupling finding reaches the cluster, and carries the label marking it as elc's own heuristic rather than a published standard.

test.name: HLR-105: every member of a recursive cycle is annotated
test.purpose: Both mutually recursive functions carry the mark and the finding, for the reason both members of a dependency cycle do.

test.name: HLR-100: a critical annotation does not become an exit status
test.purpose: A run full of critical findings in which every file was read still exits 0. Severity is a label, and drawing it on a graph does not change that.

test.name: a forward declaration is not a node
test.purpose: Three nodes and not four, which also pins that the C module's function query captures definitions rather than declarations.

test.name: HLR-106: the exported graph matches the expected topology exactly
test.purpose: The emitted GraphML is compared node for node and edge for edge against a file written from the source, so a change in what elc believes about the code appears as a diff rather than as a number nobody questions.

test.name: HLR-106: the export is off unless asked for
test.purpose: No GraphML file appears without the option, whatever the output path.

test.name: HLR-106: no companion is written when the report goes to stdout
test.purpose: Requesting the export while the report goes to standard output writes no file, since there is no output path from which to derive its name.

test.name: LLR-GML-03: the companion is named from the report by substitution
test.purpose: An output of analysis.md yields analysis.graphml and not analysis.md.graphml.

test.name: HLR-085: repeated calls are one edge carrying a call-site count
test.purpose: Two calls from one function to one helper produce a single edge with a count of two, so fan-out is distinct callees.

test.name: HLR-074: a global links its writer to its reader across files
test.purpose: A writer in one file and a reader in another are joined by an edge naming the object, though neither names the other.

test.name: HLR-074: call edges and global edges are distinguishable
test.purpose: The export carries the two kinds separately and never merged, so an analysis can tell coupling through state from coupling through calls.

test.name: HLR-096: a function whose address is taken is marked
test.purpose: A function assigned to a pointer without being called is marked a reachability root, and the function that installs it is not.

test.name: HLR-077: an unresolvable call is counted, not fatal
test.purpose: A library call and an ambiguous Ada construct are counted as unresolved and the run still succeeds.

test.name: HLR-077: the unresolved count reaches the report
test.purpose: The project summary states the count, so a reader can judge the graph's completeness without reading the export.

test.name: HLR-077: no destination is invented for an unresolved call
test.purpose: The edge count is exactly what the fixture header accounts for; a tool guessing at an unresolved target would have more.

test.name: the Ada array-index ambiguity is unresolved, not a spurious edge
test.purpose: An Ada array index that the grammar cannot distinguish from a call resolves against no subprogram and lands in the unresolved count rather than becoming an edge — pinning behaviour that is better than doc/notes.md §2.2 predicted.

test.name: an Ada call resolves like any other
test.purpose: An unambiguous Ada call still produces its edge, so the language's ambiguity costs precision on the ambiguous construct alone.

test.name: HLR-033: node identifiers follow sorted file order
test.purpose: The exported node order is the sorted-path order of the files, which is not the order a directory walk yields them in.

test.name: HLR-032: two runs over the same tree produce identical GraphML
test.purpose: The export is byte-identical across runs, so no container's internal enumeration reaches the output.

test.name: HLR-076: the graph is built without reopening a source file
test.purpose: Each source is opened exactly once under strace while the graph is built, so cross-file resolution uses the facts of the single parse rather than re-reading.

test.name: HLR-002: the repository route yields exactly the tracked source files
test.purpose: The analysed set of a repository target is exactly the tracked, non-binary, non-hidden source files, matching the set counted by hand in the fixture's header.

test.name: the hand-counted repository totals match
test.purpose: The file count and physical line total for the repository target match the values counted by hand in the fixture's header.

test.name: HLR-003: an untracked file is excluded
test.purpose: A perfectly ordinary source file that the filesystem walk would find is absent from the result, its only disqualification being that it is not in the tree at `HEAD`.

test.name: HLR-003: a gitignored build directory is excluded
test.purpose: Generated output under an ignored directory is excluded, which is where a filesystem walk goes wrong by the largest margin.

test.name: HLR-003: .gitignore is never read to decide this
test.purpose: Deleting `.gitignore` changes nothing about the result, so the exclusion follows from what git tracks rather than from elc parsing the ignore rules — which it would then have to keep in agreement with git across nested files, negations, and `core.excludesFile`.

test.name: HLR-003: a tracked file with binary content is excluded despite its extension
test.purpose: A tracked file named `.c` whose content is binary is excluded, and the extension list is shown not to contain `.c`, so git's own content check is what excluded it.

test.name: HLR-005: the exclusions of the filesystem walk apply to this route too
test.purpose: A tracked file with an excluded extension, and tracked hidden entries, are absent from the repository route's result, so the two routes agree about exclusions git is happy to report.

test.name: HLR-126: naming a subdirectory analyses that subdirectory and nothing above it
test.purpose: A subdirectory target yields the files beneath it alone, though the tree at `HEAD` is the whole repository.

test.name: HLR-126: the scoped totals are the subdirectory's, not the repository's
test.purpose: The scoped file count and line total differ from the whole repository's, so a missing scope test fails here rather than inflating a figure nobody questions.

test.name: HLR-126: a directory denotes the same files by either route
test.purpose: The same directory enumerated from the repository and then, with the repository removed, traversed from the filesystem, yields the same file set — the property the scoping requirement exists to guarantee, asserted against both routes rather than inferred from one.

test.name: HLR-004: a directory in no repository is walked at the filesystem level
test.purpose: A directory outside any repository reports the filesystem route.

test.name: HLR-002: an enclosing repository that does not track the target is disregarded
test.purpose: A gitignored build directory inside a work tree reports the filesystem route and yields its contents, rather than reporting an empty result indistinguishable from a directory with no source in it.

test.name: HLR-002: a directory tracked by no repository above it falls back
test.purpose: A freshly created directory inside a work tree — the version-controlled home directory reduced to its essential shape — reports the filesystem route and is analysed.

test.name: HLR-002: a repository with no commits falls back rather than failing
test.purpose: A repository whose `HEAD` resolves to nothing is treated as inapplicable rather than as an error, since a freshly initialised repository is an ordinary state.

test.name: HLR-127: the route is reported for each directory target
test.purpose: A run over a repository target and a plain directory reports a Discovery section naming each target with the route applied to it.

test.name: HLR-072: one directory named twice is one row, canonically spelled
test.purpose: Two spellings of one directory produce a single Discovery row naming its canonical path, so the section reports directories rather than arguments and agrees with a Files section that has already collapsed them.

test.name: HLR-033: the discovery section does not depend on the order of the targets
test.purpose: The same two targets in either order produce identical reports, so the Discovery section is ordered by a key rather than by the order the user typed.

test.name: HLR-006: a repository target produces the same report shape as any other
test.purpose: A repository target and a plain directory target produce the same section headings, completing a claim the man page has made since Phase 5 of which only the file and plain-directory halves were tested.

test.name: HLR-056: the record carries the route, so regeneration is the same report
test.purpose: A report regenerated from a record is byte-identical to a direct run, and exactly one line of it names the target with its route — so the routes survived the round trip rather than both reports being equally empty.

test.name: the hand-counted determinism totals match
test.purpose: The file count and physical line total match the values counted by hand in the fixture's header.

test.name: HLR-033: files are presented in byte order, not creation order
test.purpose: The reported paths are in ascending byte order, though the tree was created in a different one.

test.name: HLR-032: two runs over the same target are byte-identical
test.purpose: Repeating an unmodified run over the fixture tree produces identical bytes.

test.name: HLR-033: two directory targets in either order agree
test.purpose: Two overlapping directory targets produce the same report whichever order they are named in.

test.name: HLR-033: a file target and a directory target in either order agree
test.purpose: The independence of target order holds across the two classification routes, not only within one of them.

test.name: HLR-039: decoys in the working directory, the target, and an ancestor change nothing
test.purpose: Configuration-like files planted in all three locations produce output byte-identical to their absence.

test.name: HLR-039: a decoy does not change the file count either
test.purpose: A decoy planted in the target does not appear in the report as a discovered file.

test.name: HLR-040: the binary links no interpreter or virtual machine
test.purpose: The link line is checked against an allowlist; a language runtime appearing there is what the requirement forbids.

test.name: HLR-040: elc makes no network syscall
test.purpose: `strace -e trace=%network` over a full run logs no network syscall. This observes the syscalls directly rather than inferring the property from survival inside an isolated network namespace: it proves `elc` never *attempts* network access, and it runs in containers where unprivileged user namespaces are unavailable.

test.name: HLR-041: /proc reports a single thread while elc runs
test.purpose: The running process reports exactly one thread. Redirecting the report into a FIFO removes the race that made this observation impossible before: opening a FIFO for writing blocks until a reader arrives, so the sample is taken while elc is certainly alive.

test.name: HLR-041: elc issues no thread-creating syscall
test.purpose: No clone or clone3 syscall is observed for the whole run, which is stronger than sampling a thread count because it holds for every instant rather than the one sampled.

test.name: HLR-041: elc links no threading library
test.purpose: No threading library appears on the link line.

test.name: LLR-DOT-02: elc links no Graphviz library
test.purpose: Graphviz renders the output; elc writes it. Plain text emission is what keeps Graphviz a tool the user may run on the result rather than a dependency of producing it, and a link check is how that claim stays true.

test.name: LLR-DOT-02: writing the call tree spawns no process
test.purpose: The half a link check cannot make: a real run that writes a call tree issues one execve, the kernel's own, so elc does not shell out to dot either.

test.name: HLR-041: elc references no thread-creation symbol
test.purpose: No thread-creation symbol is referenced by the binary.

test.name: the build's required flags survive an overridden CFLAGS
test.purpose: The language standard, the warning set, and the header-dependency generation all appear in the compile command when CFLAGS is overridden from the command line, so a build invoked with an added flag is compiled under the same rules as one invoked with none.

test.name: HLR-041: the build passes no threading flag
test.purpose: The build never passes -pthread, which would silently license a future thread.

test.name: the help block and the real target set agree
test.purpose: Every declared target appears in the makefile's help block and every name in that block is a real target, so the hand-maintained summary cannot drift from what the build actually offers.

test.name: make help prints the block from the file's header
test.purpose: The help target prints the header block itself, marker stripped, so a reader who opens the file and a reader who runs it see one text.

test.name: every grammar is linked with the scanner it requires
test.purpose: No delivered grammar has an unresolved external-scanner symbol. The rule located an optional scanner with a construct make expands before running the recipe, so it looked for a file the fetch above it had not unpacked and silently found none — invisible while C, which has no scanner, was the only grammar.

test.name: the grammar build takes its owner and reference as parameters
test.purpose: The rule for a grammar hosted outside the parsing library's organisation reaches that owner, and fetches by commit rather than by tag because its upstream cuts no releases. Both would be impossible with either value hardcoded.

test.name: every grammar the build declares is one the build can produce
test.purpose: Each name the build lists has a rule behind it. A missing one fails only on a clean tree, which is the tree nobody builds on.

test.name: check-prereqs reports every grammar against upstream
test.purpose: Each delivered language appears in the dependency report, so a pin that is immutable is not thereby invisible when it falls behind.

test.name: check-prereqs survives an unreachable upstream
test.purpose: An unreachable upstream reports "unknown" rather than failing or hanging: the report is a diagnostic a person runs, not a gate.

test.name: every runtime data file the build does not produce is tracked
test.purpose: Every file under the runtime location that the build does not itself produce is tracked by the repository, so that a version-control ignore rule cannot silently exclude product data. `.gitignore` carries `*.map` for linker map files, which also matched the extension table: it worked locally, was absent from the clone CI made, and every parsing test then failed naming the missing file rather than the rule that hid it.

test.name: HLR-043: elc does not modify the tree it analyses
test.purpose: The analysed tree checksums identically before and after a run.

test.name: HLR-043: elc opens nothing for writing
test.purpose: No syscall capable of modifying a file — an open carrying a writing mode, a creat, an unlink, a truncate, or a rename — is observed for the whole run. This is direct evidence of read-only operation, where comparing checksums afterwards is only circumstantial.

test.name: HLR-076: each source file is opened exactly once
test.purpose: No source file is opened twice for the whole run, which is the observable form of the single-parse rule: a second open would mean some stage re-read it.

test.name: HLR-009: the grammar is loaded from the runtime location, not linked
test.purpose: No grammar appears among the binary's link-time dependencies, and the grammar file is opened during the run — language support is loaded at run time rather than compiled in.

test.name: HLR-043: elc runs against a read-only directory
test.purpose: A run succeeds against a directory with write permission removed.

test.name: HLR-125: the local sanitizer gate is as strong as the pipeline's
test.purpose: The sanitizer options the local target sets and those the pipeline sets are the same, and both abort on error. Without aborting, a leak reported inside a forked test child never reaches the parent's exit status, so a leaking unit test passes locally and fails only in CI — which is how Phase 11 shipped two of them.

test.name: the fixture level is wired and elc is runnable
test.purpose: The fixture-conformance level is wired and green before the first real fixture is written.

test.name: every expected-value file has a fixture header beside it
test.purpose: Guards the convention that expected values are hand-counted, never generated from elc's own output.
